subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]
passage: I am Shalini and I sit next to Arohi in art class. Last Monday she told me she was starting to draw for real. I expected a huge plan, but she said, "Ten minutes a day, that is all. My cousin planned two hours daily and stopped by Thursday. A tiny habit that carries on beats a big one that dies." Every afternoon after that I saw her at the window seat with her sketchbook and a timer on the sill, drawing pots and shoes until it beeped. She stopped even when she was halfway through a leaf. By the third week her sketchbook was fat. I cannot tell if she ever wanted to do more; she just kept going.

qa.q: How many minutes a day did Arohi decide to draw?
qa.a: Arohi decided to draw for ten minutes a day.

qa.q: What was Arohi worried about when she chose such a small amount?
qa.a: That a big plan would fail after a few days, as her cousin's did, so she wanted a habit that would carry on.

qa.q: What could Arohi do when ten minutes starts to feel easy?
qa.a: Add a few minutes slowly or set a small goal, such as one finished drawing a week, because growth stays steady that way.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Arohi stopping halfway through a leaf?
qa.a: With some puzzlement and admiration for the discipline, though Shalini admits she cannot tell whether Arohi wanted to do more.

grounding: A girl beginning drawing chooses ten minutes a day, judging a small habit that continues better than a big plan that stops.

subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday. Dilnaz opens the sketchbook Tanuja Khala gave her for Eid. Last summer she promised herself an hour of kathak every day and stopped on day three, sore and bored. "Not an hour this time," she tells herself. "Ten minutes. Even on test days I have ten minutes. Small is fine, as long as it doesn't stop." She sets the kitchen timer and draws the teapot.
Thursday. School ran late and she is yawning. She almost skips, then thinks, ten minutes is shorter than one cartoon. She draws the cat asleep on the chair.
Three weeks later. Tanuja Khala flips through the book: teapots, cats, Abbu's slippers. "You've drawn every day?" Dilnaz nods. "Every day. Just not for very long."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz draw on Thursday?
qa.a: She drew the cat asleep on the chair.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when she remembered the kathak plan?
qa.a: She felt a little disappointed in herself for quitting on day three, and wanted a plan small enough that she would not give up again.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz try if ten minutes starts to feel too easy?
qa.a: She could add a few minutes on weekends only, growing slowly so the daily habit never breaks.

qa.q: How might Tanuja Khala feel flipping through the sketchbook?
qa.a: She is likely pleased and a little surprised to see her Eid gift used every single day, even if each drawing is small 😊.

grounding: Shows a girl choosing ten minutes of drawing a day because a small habit that lasts beats a big plan that stops.

subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]
passage: Chetan beta, you want to draw like me? Then hear how your Zeenat Aunty started, back when she was nine and owned one pencil. My friend Shabnam and I got drawing books in the same week. Shabnam made a grand plan: two hours every evening, a new portrait each day. I looked at my evenings, full of homework and fetching water, and I thought, two hours will break by Wednesday. So I said ten minutes, right after the evening prayer, every single day. Shabnam's plan lasted three evenings. Mine lasted, well, look at these hands. Some days ten minutes was only one leaf. But a leaf every day for a year makes a whole tree, beta.

qa.q: When did young Zeenat set aside her ten minutes?
qa.a: Right after the evening prayer, every single day.

qa.q: Why did young Zeenat choose ten minutes instead of two hours?
qa.a: She was worried about her busy evenings of homework and fetching water, and wanted a habit that would not break by Wednesday.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat fitted the drawing to her real evenings instead of an ideal plan; ten minutes survived busy days, while Shabnam's two hours collapsed after three evenings.

qa.q: How might Shabnam have felt when her plan stopped after three evenings?
qa.a: Shabnam may have felt disappointed or discouraged, since a grand plan that breaks early can make someone feel they have failed at drawing itself.

grounding: An elder recalls starting drawing with ten minutes a day, knowing a small lasting habit beats a big plan that stops.
